nodes.label: Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
nodes.one_line: Name the cognitive level a goal actually requires, so 'understand' stops being where every objective quietly lands.
know_what: Revised Bloom's Taxonomy — six cognitive process categories (remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create) crossed with four knowledge types (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive)
Cognitive process vs. knowledge dimension — the two-dimensional structure that replaced the original one-dimensional 1956 taxonomy
Verb-to-level mapping — the standard verb lists (list, explain, apply, differentiate, justify, design) used to signal which level an objective targets
Level creep — the tendency for objectives to cluster at 'understand' or 'apply' because they're easy to write, even when the real target is higher
Affective and psychomotor domains — Krathwohl's affective taxonomy and Simpson's psychomotor taxonomy, used when the goal isn't purely cognitive
Taxonomy as a design tool, not a grading rubric — its main use is choosing the right verb and activity type, not scoring after the fact
know_how: Classify a stated goal by its actual cognitive process level, not by the verb someone happened to use to describe it
Select an objective verb from the level-appropriate verb list instead of defaulting to 'understand'
Cross a cognitive process level with a knowledge type to fully specify what the objective demands
Check a course's full objective list for level creep — an unusual cluster at 'remember' or 'apply' when the job task demands 'evaluate' or 'create'
Use the affective or psychomotor taxonomy instead of forcing a values or motor-skill goal into the cognitive taxonomy
Explain a taxonomy classification choice to an SME in plain terms so they can sanity-check it against the real job
habits: Ask 'what would doing this at the create/evaluate level actually look like' before settling for 'apply'
Notice when every objective in a course landed on the same two levels
Treat the taxonomy as a checking tool applied after a draft, not a fill-in-the-blank template
Match the taxonomy's knowledge type to the objective, not just the process level
Double-check a level classification against what the real job task demands, not just the wording of the goal statement
nodes.checkpoint: Given five stated learning goals, classify each by cognitive process level and knowledge type using the revised Bloom's Taxonomy, and rewrite any goal misclassified by its own verb.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the taxonomy as a vocabulary list to make objectives sound more official, picking a high-level verb like 'analyze' for what's actually a remember-level task.
sources: Anderson & Krathwohl (eds.), A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing

nodes.label: Prerequisite Mapping
nodes.one_line: Order objectives by what a learner genuinely needs first, not by the order topics appear in the source material.
know_what: Prerequisite relationship — objective B requires objective A's skill or knowledge as an input, distinct from merely being related in topic
Learning hierarchy (Gagné) — a structure built by asking what the learner would need to already know to learn this, recursively from the terminal objective down
Topic order vs. dependency order — the difference between how a textbook groups material and the actual order a learner needs to acquire it
Entry behavior — what a learner is assumed to already know coming into a course, which sets the bottom of the prerequisite map
Gap in the chain — a prerequisite the target audience doesn't actually have, discovered by comparing the map to the audience profile
Redundant prerequisite — a listed dependency the audience already reliably has, which can be dropped from the course without risk
know_how: Start from the terminal objective and recursively ask what a learner would need to already be able to do to learn this, until reaching entry behavior
Build a learning hierarchy diagram showing objectives as nodes and prerequisite relationships as directed links
Compare the bottom of the hierarchy against the audience profile to find gaps that need to be taught, not assumed
Cut a prerequisite from the course scope when the audience profile confirms they reliably already have it
Resequence a course's topic order when the dependency map contradicts the source material's chapter order
Validate a contested prerequisite link with an SME instead of assuming the intuitive order is the dependency order
habits: Ask what a learner would need to already know to do that, recursively, not just once
Check the source material's chapter order against the dependency map instead of trusting it by default
Flag an objective with no clear prerequisite as either genuinely foundational or under-analyzed
Re-verify entry behavior against real audience data instead of an assumed baseline
Redraw the hierarchy when a pilot reveals the assumed entry behavior was wrong
nodes.checkpoint: Build a learning hierarchy for a terminal objective with at least three prerequisite levels, and identify one prerequisite gap where the target audience profile doesn't match the assumed entry behavior.
nodes.common_failure: Sequencing a course by the order topics appear in a reference document or textbook instead of by actual dependency, so learners hit a concept before they have what they need to learn it.
sources: Robert Gagné, The Conditions of Learning
Van Merriënboer, Ten Steps to Complex Learning

nodes.label: Backward Design Mapping
nodes.one_line: Decide what counts as evidence of mastery before designing a single activity, so the activities can't drift from the goal.
know_what: Understanding by Design (UbD) — Wiggins & McTighe's three-stage backward design: identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, plan learning experiences
Six facets of understanding — explain, interpret, apply, have perspective, empathize, self-assess; UbD's expanded target beyond simple recall
Essential question — an open, recurring question that frames a unit and can't be answered in one sentence, used to anchor genuine understanding goals
Enduring understanding — the big idea meant to outlast the course itself, distinct from a fact that will be forgotten
Evidence-first sequencing — designing the assessment (stage 2) before the learning activities (stage 3), the discipline that gives backward design its name
Twin sins of design — Wiggins & McTighe's term for activity-focused design (fun but aimless) and coverage-focused design (comprehensive but shallow)
know_how: Write the desired results (objectives, essential questions, enduring understandings) for a unit before touching any activity ideas
Draft the assessment evidence for stage 2 immediately after stage 1, resisting the pull to jump to activity design
Check a unit plan against the twin sins: is it a fun activity with no clear evidence trail, or comprehensive coverage with no depth
Write at least one essential question per unit that a learner couldn't fully answer on day one
Sequence stage 3 learning experiences only after stages 1 and 2 are locked, so activities serve the evidence, not the reverse
Use the six facets of understanding to check whether an objective is asking for real understanding or just recall dressed up
habits: Resist the pull to brainstorm activities first — that's the twin sin backward design exists to prevent
Ask what would count as evidence of this before designing anything a learner will do
Check whether a unit's essential question actually has more than one defensible answer
Notice when a plan is really a coverage list wearing a unit-plan's structure
Keep the three stages visibly separate in the document so the sequence can't quietly collapse
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a three-stage backward design document for one unit: desired results with an essential question, assessment evidence, and a learning-experience outline, completed in that order.
nodes.common_failure: Designing engaging activities first and writing objectives and assessments afterward to match them, which produces a course that feels busy but can't demonstrate what it actually taught.
sources: Grant Wiggins & Jay McTighe, Understanding by Design
Wiggins & McTighe, 'twin sins' of design essays

nodes.label: Objective Review & Critique
nodes.one_line: Catch an objective that's actually an activity, a topic, or an unmeasurable feeling wearing an objective's syntax.
know_what: Objective vs. activity — an objective states what the learner can do; an activity describes what they'll be doing during the lesson, and the two get conflated constantly
Objective vs. topic — 'the four phases of onboarding' is a topic; 'sequence the four phases of onboarding for a new hire' is an objective
Compound objective — an objective silently containing two or more behaviors joined by 'and', which should usually be split
Unmeasurable modifier — words like 'effectively', 'thoroughly', or 'appropriately' that sound like a criterion but specify nothing checkable
SMART-for-objectives checklist — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, adapted as a review checklist rather than a writing template
Reviewer's rewrite pass — the practice of rewriting a flagged objective on the spot to demonstrate the fix, not just naming the problem
know_how: Test a draft objective by asking whether it states a topic, an activity, or a behavior, and reclassify accordingly
Split a compound objective joined by 'and' into two separate objectives with their own criteria
Flag any unmeasurable modifier and replace it with a stated, checkable criterion
Run a full objective list through a SMART checklist pass before it goes to an SME for content review
Rewrite a flagged objective immediately during review instead of only noting that it's weak
Check that an objective's verb matches its intended Bloom's level, not just that it has a verb
habits: Read an objective and ask whether it's a topic, an activity, or a behavior before anything else
Circle every 'and' in an objective list as a likely compound-objective flag
Distrust any objective that reads well but that you couldn't write a test item for
Rewrite on the spot instead of just marking an objective as weak
Check a reviewed objective's verb against its intended Bloom's level before signing off
nodes.checkpoint: Given a list of ten draft objectives with mixed problems — topics, activities, compound objectives, unmeasurable modifiers — correctly flag each problem type and rewrite at least six into fully specified behavioral objectives.
nodes.common_failure: Approving an objective because it uses the right sentence structure and an approved verb, without checking whether it's actually specific and measurable underneath the format.

nodes.label: Curriculum Mapping
nodes.one_line: See the whole multi-module curriculum at once well enough to find the gaps and the redundant repeats.
know_what: Curriculum map — a document showing every module's objectives, assessments, and estimated duration across a full multi-module program
Vertical alignment — objectives across modules building on each other in dependency order, checked at the whole-curriculum level rather than module by module
Horizontal redundancy — the same objective or content taught in two different modules without either module referencing the other, wasting learner time
Coverage gap — a competency the program is supposed to build toward that no module's objectives actually address
Curriculum-level pacing — cumulative hours across modules checked against the time the audience realistically has, not just each module's individual budget
Map review cadence — a scheduled point, such as annually or at each major content change, to re-check the map instead of letting it silently drift out of date
know_how: Build a spreadsheet or diagram listing every module's objectives, mapped against the overall program's terminal competencies
Trace vertical alignment by checking that every module's entry behavior is covered by an earlier module's objectives
Scan for horizontal redundancy by comparing objective wording across modules, not just module titles
Identify coverage gaps by checking the program's terminal competencies against the full objective list and flagging anything missing
Total cumulative hours across the mapped curriculum and check it against the audience's actual available time
Schedule a recurring review of the curriculum map so it stays a living document instead of a one-time artifact
habits: Look at the whole program map before approving a single new module's objectives
Ask whether a new module actually needs the prerequisites it assumes, or if it's re-teaching something covered earlier
Total the hours across the whole map periodically, not just per module
Treat a stale curriculum map as a problem to fix immediately, not a documentation nicety
Compare objective wording, not just titles, when checking for redundancy across modules
nodes.checkpoint: Given the objective lists for four related modules, produce a curriculum map that identifies at least one vertical alignment gap and one horizontal redundancy across the modules.
nodes.common_failure: Designing each module in isolation to its own brief, so the finished program has modules that silently duplicate content and others that assume a prerequisite no earlier module actually taught.
sources: L. Dee Fink, Creating Significant Learning Experiences

nodes.label: Competency Framework Alignment
nodes.one_line: Map a course's objectives onto an external competency or certification framework without warping either one to fit.
know_what: Competency framework — an externally defined set of competencies, from a certification body, industry standard, or internal job architecture, a course is meant to build toward
Crosswalk — a document mapping a course's objectives to a framework's competencies, showing coverage and gaps in both directions
Framework granularity mismatch — a common problem where a framework's competencies are broader or narrower than a course's objectives, requiring judgment to align rather than a clean one-to-one match
Certification constraint — when a framework is tied to a certification exam, the exam blueprint's weighting becomes a hard constraint on the course's own emphasis, not just a reference
Framework versioning — frameworks get revised on their own schedule, and a course aligned to an old version can silently drift out of compliance
Over-alignment risk — designing a course purely to a framework's checklist at the expense of the actual diagnosed performance gap
know_how: Build a two-directional crosswalk: every course objective mapped to a framework competency, and every framework competency mapped to a course objective or flagged as a gap
Resolve a granularity mismatch by splitting or merging objectives to align with the framework's actual grain, documenting the judgment call
Weight course emphasis to match a certification exam's published blueprint when the course exists to prepare learners for that exam
Check the framework's version and revision date against the course's alignment documentation at each course review cycle
Flag when framework alignment is pulling objectives away from the diagnosed performance gap, and resolve the conflict explicitly rather than silently favoring the framework
Present the crosswalk to the framework's certifying body or internal owner for validation before finalizing
habits: Check the framework's version date before trusting an existing alignment document
Ask whether an objective exists because of the diagnosed gap or because the framework demands it, when the two pull in different directions
Treat a framework crosswalk as living documentation that needs a re-check on a schedule, not a one-time deliverable
Push back when strict framework alignment would produce an objective the actual audience gap doesn't need
Validate a contested crosswalk mapping with the framework's own owner instead of guessing at intent

know_why.claim: A course tied to an external competency or certification framework should weight its content to match the framework's published blueprint.
know_why.because: learners and sponsors are relying on the course to prepare for a specific external standard, and misweighting it undermines that promise
know_why.disputed_by: performance-consulting practitioners who argue framework alignment can pull a course toward testing the framework's checklist instead of closing the organization's actual diagnosed performance gap
know_why.source: certification-preparation ID practice vs. Robert Brinkerhoff and performance-consulting critiques of framework-driven design

nodes.checkpoint: Produce a two-directional crosswalk between a course's objectives and an external competency framework's competencies, with every gap in either direction named and a resolution proposed.
nodes.common_failure: Aligning a course to a framework by matching titles and keywords instead of actual competency content, producing a crosswalk that looks complete but doesn't hold up under a certifying body's own review.
sources: Robert Brinkerhoff, performance-consulting critiques of framework-driven training
